  • F−1(U) ~ X for U ~ Uniform(0,1) — the inverse c.d.f. turns uniform noise into any distribution you want.

The second half is inverse transform sampling: your machine generates uniform random numbers, and this converts them into samples from any distribution with an invertible c.d.f.

Example: for Expo(λ), F(x) = 1 − e−λx, so F−1(u) = −ln(1−u)/λ. Draw u uniform, apply that, and you have an exponential sample.

r.rot: every distribution is secretly a uniform in a costume, and the c.d.f. is the costume. push X through its own c.d.f. and it flattens to uniform — every time, any distribution. run it backwards and uniform noise becomes whatever you want. your computer only knows how to make uniform randomness. this theorem is how it makes everything else.
r.ex: Exponential: u → −ln(1−u)/λ. That one line is inside `numpy.random.exponential`. Same trick underlies the samplers in your Sampling and Metropolis labs.
r.why: It's the bridge from theory to your keyboard. Combined with §1.10's Monte Carlo results, it's the full story of how simulation works: uniform bits in, arbitrary distributions out, sample means approximating anything you want.
r.math: P(F(X) ≤ u) = P(X ≤ F<sup>−1</sup>(u)) = F(F<sup>−1</sup>(u)) = u, which is the Uniform(0,1) c.d.f.

cards.q: Give the multivariate change-of-variables formula for densities. What does it say about linear maps of a normal?
cards.a:
Let Y = Φ(X) with Φ : Rn → Rn a diffeomorphism (C¹ with C¹ inverse Ψ = Φ−1). For measurable A with B = Φ(A),
∫A fX(x)dx = P(X∈A) = P(Y∈B) = ∫B fY(y)dy
and the general change-of-variables formula turns the left side into ∫B(fX∘Ψ)(y)|det DΨ|dy. Since this holds for every A:
fY(y) = (fX ∘ Ψ)(y) · |det DΨ|
The Jacobian determinant is the volume-stretching factor — densities are per unit volume, so squeezing space must raise the density to keep total probability at 1.

Example 2.9.9 — linear maps of a normal. Let X ~ N(μ,Σ) and Y = AX with A invertible. Then Ψ is multiplication by A−1, |det DΨ| = |det A|−1, and using |AΣAT| = |A|²|Σ| the algebra collapses to

Y ~ N( Aμ, AΣAT )
The normal family is closed under invertible linear maps, with the mean and covariance transforming exactly as you'd hope.

r.rot: change variables and the density has to pick up a jacobian. reason: a density is probability per unit volume, so if your map squashes a region to half its size, the density there must double or you lose probability. that's the |det DΨ| factor, nothing more. the headline consequence: apply any invertible matrix to a multivariate normal and you get another multivariate normal, mean Aμ, covariance AΣAT. normals are closed under linear maps, which is a big part of why they're so easy to work with.
r.ex: Example 2.9.10 is the impressive one. For independent gammas R ~ Gamma(a,λ) and S ~ Gamma(b,λ), transform to U = R+S and V = R/(R+S). The Jacobian is −u, and the resulting joint density factors — proving that U ~ Gamma(a+b,λ) and V ~ Beta(a,b) are independent. Sum and ratio, gamma and beta, independent of each other.
r.why: The one-dimensional |dg<sup>−1</sup>/dy| from Prop 2.9.1 is just this with n = 1. And the same Jacobian is what makes transformation invariance a real question for priors — it's exactly the factor that MAX ENT fails to respect (Unexample 4.7.6) and that the Jeffreys prior is built to absorb (Thm 4.7.11).
r.math: f<sub>Y</sub>(y) = f<sub>X</sub>(Ψ(y))|det DΨ(y)|, Ψ = Φ<sup>−1</sup>. X ~ N(μ,Σ), Y = AX ⇒ Y ~ N(Aμ, AΣA<sup>T</sup>).

cards.q: What is the distribution of a sum of two independent random variables?
cards.a:
Proposition 2.9.11 (discrete). For independent X, Y on S with p.m.f.s gX, gY, the sum Z = X + Y has p.m.f. the convolution
gZ(z) = (gX * gY)(z) = ∑x∈S gX(x) gY(z − x)
The proof is one line of conditioning: P(X+Y=z) = ∑xP(X=x)P(X+Y=z | X=x) = ∑xP(X=x)P(Y=z−x), using independence at the last step.

Proposition 2.9.12 (continuous). Same formula with an integral:

fZ(z) = (fX * fY)(z) = ∫S fX(x) fY(z − x) dx
The proof goes through the c.d.f., substitutes ζ = x + y in the inner integral to decouple the limits, swaps the order, and differentiates.

Nota Bene 2.9.13 — the support trap. Even when x and ζ are in the support S, that does not mean ζ − x is. The integrand must be taken as 0 wherever ζ − x is outside the support of Y.

Forgetting this is the standard way to get a wrong answer for a sum of, say, two uniforms or two exponentials.

r.rot: adding independent random variables convolves their distributions: to land on z, you need X = x and Y = z−x, so sum (or integrate) that product over every x. that's it. the practical warning is about limits — the formula looks like it integrates over everything, but fY(z−x) is zero whenever z−x falls outside Y's support, and if you don't chop the integral there you get nonsense. for two uniforms on [0,1], for instance, the answer is a triangle, and you only get the triangle by respecting the cutoffs.
r.ex: This is the reason characteristic functions matter so much (§4.2). Convolution is painful and compounds badly: adding n variables means n−1 nested convolutions. Under φ<sub>X+Y</sub> = φ<sub>X</sub>φ<sub>Y</sub> it becomes a single product, or a power for i.i.d. copies.
r.why: It is the operation the central limit theorem is secretly about: S<sub>n</sub> is an n-fold convolution of the parent density with itself, and the CLT says that repeated convolution smooths anything into a Gaussian. Seeing it as convolution is what makes that plausible.
r.math: g<sub>X+Y</sub> = g<sub>X</sub> * g<sub>Y</sub>; f<sub>X+Y</sub>(z) = ∫f<sub>X</sub>(x)f<sub>Y</sub>(z−x)dx. Integrand is 0 where z−x ∉ supp(Y). Needs independence.

cards.q: When symbolic inversion fails, how do you get the distribution of Y = Φ(X)? Define the standard error.
cards.a:
Symbolic inversion is often difficult or impossible, and then the change-of-variables formula is useless. The Monte Carlo alternative is almost embarrassingly simple:
If x₁,…,xn are draws from X, then yi = Φ(xi) are draws from Y.
Just push your samples through the function. From those you estimate E[Y] ≈ ȳ, Var(Y) ≈ (1/n)∑(yi−ȳ)², P(Y ≤ y) ≈ (1/n)∑1yi≤y, and the median as the sample median.

How accurate? The CLT says μ̂ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n), so by the 68-95-99.7 rule it lies within one σ/√n of μ about 68% of the time. That quantity is the standard error:

SE = σ/√n ≈ ŝx/√n,  where ŝ²x = (1/(n−1))∑(xi−x̄)²
(σ is unknown too, so use the unbiased sample variance.) A Monte Carlo estimate lies within two standard errors of the truth with about 95% probability.

Example 2.9.14. X ~ Uniform([0,1]), estimate E[X²] with n = 10⁶: ȳ = 0.333298, ŝ²y = 0.088995, so SE = 0.0003. The true value is ∫₀¹x²dx = 1/3, and |ȳ − μ| ≈ 0.000035 — well within one standard error.

r.rot: if you can't invert the function symbolically, don't. sample X, apply Φ to every sample, and you now have samples of Y. everything you wanted — mean, variance, quantiles, probabilities — comes out of that list. and you get an error bar for free: the standard error σ/√n, estimated with the sample standard deviation. two standard errors is your 95% window. note the √n again — a hundred times more samples buys you ten times the precision, which is why monte carlo is easy to start and expensive to make precise.
r.ex: §2.9.5's Box–Muller method is the case where a dedicated trick beats brute force. The normal has no convenient inverse c.d.f., so instead you generate a bivariate normal in polar coordinates: rotational symmetry makes θ ~ Uniform([0,2π)), and R² ~ Gamma(1,½) is exponential, so R² = −2log(U₁) and θ = 2πU₂ give two independent standard normals from two uniforms.
r.why: It closes the section honestly: inversion sampling (§2.9.1) works when F<sup>−1</sup> is known, change of variables works when Φ is invertible in closed form, and when neither holds you simulate — and the standard error tells you how much to trust the result.
r.math: y<sub>i</sub> = Φ(x<sub>i</sub>) are draws from Y. SE = σ/√n ≈ ŝ<sub>x</sub>/√n. P(|ȳ − E[h(X)]| ≤ 2ŝ<sub>y</sub>/√n) ≈ 95%.
